A sitcom is a type of television (or radio) show built around a fixed group of characters who keep finding themselves in funny, awkward, or absurd situations. The word is short for situation comedy — a comedy that gets its humor from situations, meaning the circumstances and events the characters are caught up in, rather than from stand-up jokes or one-liners delivered to the audience.

The heart of a sitcom is this: you take a small, familiar group of people, place them in a setting they return to again and again (a home, an office, a coffee shop), and then keep throwing problems, misunderstandings, and complications at them. The comedy (the humor) comes from how they react to those situations and from the clashes between their personalities.

Think of it like this: if you locked five very different people in an office together every day, the awkward moments, arguments, misunderstandings, and funny incidents that happen would be the raw material of a sitcom.

1. A fixed cast of recurring characters
Every sitcom has a core group of characters you see in every episode. You get to know them well — their habits, flaws, quirks, and relationships. This familiarity is part of what makes sitcoms enjoyable. When a character does something predictably foolish or stubborn, you laugh because you know them.

2. A consistent setting
The story almost always happens in the same place or places. A family home, a workplace, a pub, an apartment building — this is called the "situation." The setting is stable; the events within it change each episode.

3. Self-contained episodes
Most sitcom episodes tell a complete little story with a beginning, middle, and end — all within about 20 to 30 minutes. By the end of the episode, things usually settle back to roughly how they were. The characters don't dramatically change their lives; they reset, ready for the next episode's new mess. This is sometimes called the "status quo reset." (Some modern sitcoms break this rule and have running storylines across episodes, but the classic formula resets.)

4. Short runtime
Sitcoms are short — typically 20 to 30 minutes per episode. This is intentional. The format is designed for quick, light, repeated viewing.

5. The laugh track (or live studio audience)
Many traditional sitcoms were filmed in front of a live studio audience, so you hear real laughter after jokes. Others added a laugh track — a recorded sound of laughter edited in. This signals to the viewer: this is the funny bit. Many modern sitcoms have dropped this entirely and feel more naturalistic, like a documentary or a film.

In a sitcom, the comedy almost never comes from a character turning to the camera and telling a joke. Instead, it comes from:

  • Misunderstandings — a character hears the wrong thing, assumes the wrong thing, or says something that gets wildly misinterpreted.
  • Clashing personalities — a messy person forced to live with a neat freak; a lazy employee stuck working for a demanding boss.
  • Escalating chaos — a small problem grows bigger and bigger because characters keep making it worse, usually out of pride, fear, or foolishness.
  • Dramatic irony — the audience knows something a character doesn't, and watching them stumble around in ignorance is funny.
  • Running jokes and character quirks — a character who always says a certain phrase, always reacts in an exaggerated way, or always makes the same type of mistake.

Family sitcoms — centered on a family at home. The tensions and warmth of family life provide the situations. (Example: a classic American family sitcom.)

Workplace sitcoms — set in an office, a hospital, a police station, or any job environment. The comedy comes from the professional relationships, office politics, and the absurdity of work life. (The Office is a famous example.)

Flatmate/roommate sitcoms — a group of friends or strangers sharing a living space. The forced closeness creates conflict and comedy. (Friends is the most famous example.)

Animated sitcoms — sitcoms made as cartoons, following the same rules of fixed characters and recurring settings, but using animation instead of live actors. (The Simpsons is the most iconic.)
How a Sitcom Differs from Other Shows

—SitcomDrama SeriesSketch Comedy

A drama series tells serious, emotionally heavy stories, often with significant consequences. Characters change, face loss, and grow. A sitcom keeps things light; even when characters face a problem, the tone stays comedic and the situation resolves without lasting damage.

A sketch comedy show is a collection of short, unrelated comedy bits performed by a cast — there's no ongoing story and often no recurring characters. A sitcom, by contrast, has a continuous fictional world with the same characters living in an ongoing (if reset-every-episode) story.

A stand-up comedy special is just one comedian performing jokes for an audience with no fictional world at all. A sitcom creates a fictional world and lets humor emerge from within it.

The word situation in "situation comedy" is doing real work. It tells you that the comedy is embedded in a scenario, not imported from outside. The characters are not comedians performing for you — they are people living in a world, and you are laughing at what happens to them and because of them.

This is what separates a sitcom from other comedy formats. The situation is the stage; the characters are the players; and the comedy is what naturally erupts when you put those particular people in those particular circumstances.

A sitcom is a short, episodic comedy TV show built around the same group of characters in the same setting, where the humor comes from the situations, misunderstandings, and personality clashes the characters repeatedly experience. Each episode is roughly self-contained. The world resets after each episode. You watch to see these familiar people mess things up and muddle through — and laugh along the way.
